    Instructor Notes

    General

    • The lesson takes about 15 hours of teaching and exercises (see the front matter of each episode), so it fits a course of about 20 hours with lectures. Multi-table (multi-omics) analysis is covered by the follow-up multi-omics lesson.
    • Most of the time should be hands-on. Episodes 5–8 end with a 30-minute consolidation exercise, and the capstone (episode 10) is a 50-minute independent analysis. These are the flexible parts: shorten them if time runs out.
    • Sections and challenges marked bonus (all taxonomic ranks in one object in episode 5, clustering in episode 7) are optional. Later episodes do not depend on them.
    • Episodes 1 and 2 have no code to type. Use them to motivate the learners, walk through the workflow figure, introduce the study and discuss what to keep in mind about data generation. Episode 3 can be skipped if the learners have set up the project and downloaded the data before the workshop.
    • The episodes build on each other through the files data/tse.rds (saved in episode 4) and data/tse_processed.rds (saved in episode 5, with the relabundance and rclr tables). If a learner falls behind, they can catch up by running the “save” chunks of the earlier episodes.
    • Live-code every chunk. The chunks are kept short on purpose.

    The story of the lesson

    All episodes follow the same research question: is the gut microbiome of people with colorectal cancer (CRC) different from that of healthy people, and which bacteria differ? Two threads connect the episodes. Point them out as you go.

    The Prevotella copri thread

    • Episode 5: Prevotella dominates many healthy samples in the composition plot. The median relative abundance of P. copri is about 47 % in healthy people and about 1 % in CRC.
    • Episode 6: CRC patients have higher alpha diversity. This surprises many learners. The explanation is that the healthy samples are dominated by P. copri and are therefore less even. Use this to discuss that “higher diversity” is not automatically “healthier”.
    • Episode 7: P. copri drives the separation along the first PCoA axis.
    • Episode 8: P. copri is the strongest MaAsLin 3 result. In the simple linear model on two taxa, its effect weakens when the location is added (most people from Kerala have CRC), which shows why covariates matter.

    The location thread (confounding)

    • Episode 1 (challenge 4) introduces the idea of confounding, and episode 2 (challenge 1) the related idea of batch effects.
    • Episode 4 (challenge 4): CRC patients come from both Bhopal (a city) and Kerala (a state) (15/15), but healthy people come mostly from Bhopal (26/4). The lesson calls this variable “location”.
    • Episode 6 (challenge 6) and episode 7 (challenge 7): age is also linked to the disease (there are no CRC patients under 40). The disease effect on the composition remains when age is added to the dbRDA. Challenge 7 also shows that the order of the variables does not matter in addRDA(), because each variable is tested while the others are taken into account.
    • Episode 7: the PCoA coloured by location looks similar to the one coloured by disease. dbRDA shows that the disease effect remains when the location is included.
    • Episode 8: the location is included in the models. Challenge 3 shows that leaving it out changes the list of significant species.

    Beyond the core analyses

    • Episode 7 (bonus, clustering): hierarchical clustering on rclr values finds a Prevotella and a non-Prevotella community type, which almost matches the disease groups. Stress the callout: cluster the data, not the ordination axes.
    • Episode 8: Flavonifractor plautii, named in the title of the Gupta paper, is the clearest prevalence result.
    • Episode 9: the test set has only 12 samples, so the test AUC jumps between random splits. The challenge makes this visible.
    • Episode 10 (capstone, Tengeler2020): the results are mostly null. This is intended: not every study finds a difference.

    Differential abundance in this lesson

    • Episode 8 first shows the idea of DAA on two taxa (tse_sub): a box plot, a t-test and a linear model on log10 relative abundances (pseudocount 1 added to the counts), with simple functions from the daa package. A Student’s t-test (var.equal = TRUE) gives exactly the same p-values as a linear model with one two-group variable. Adding the location as a covariate shows what most DAA methods do under the hood. A large benchmark found that such simple methods give the most replicable results (Pelto et al. 2025).
    • After multiple testing, the episode moves to a dedicated method, MaAsLin 3, for all taxa. Its abundance model uses only the samples where a taxon is present, and its prevalence model tests presence and absence. This is why P. copri is only weakly significant in the simple linear model with location (where the zeros are included), but the strongest result of MaAsLin 3.
    • daa is installed from GitHub and is not loaded with library(); the lesson calls its functions with daa::. The current version has a bug: once the daa namespace is loaded, getPERMANOVA() fails in the same R session with subscript out of bounds. If this happens, for example in the capstone, restart R and run the earlier steps again.
    • MaAsLin 3 writes its files to the maaslin3_output folder in the project, and creates it if needed. One of its steps uses random numbers, so learners’ q-values can differ slightly from the lesson.

    Notes on the data

    • The data comes from shotgun metagenomics profiled with MetaPhlAn, through the curatedMetagenomicData package. The “counts” are estimated from MetaPhlAn’s relative abundances, not real read counts. For this reason, the lesson does not rarefy the data and shows no rarefaction curves. Episode 6 mentions rarefaction only in a callout.
    • The rclr transformation (vegan’s decostand(method = "rclr"), used by mia) fills in the zeros by OptSpace matrix completion. By default it returns the full low-rank (rank 3) reconstruction, not just the filled-in zeros. The PCA in episode 7 therefore has only three non-zero components, and single-taxon rclr values are smoothed. For this reason, the lesson plots single taxa as relative abundances, and episode 8 tests log relative abundances. Episode 5 (challenge 4) shows learners that zero counts get non-zero rclr values; use it to explain that rclr values are estimates.
    • Some taxon names look odd, for example species-_rectale, which is Eubacterium rectale (the genus name contains brackets in the original taxonomy). This comes from the original data.
    • The data is shipped in episodes/data/; see the README there for its source.

    Common problems

    • Package versions. The lesson needs the current Bioconductor release. Check with BiocManager::version(). The lesson is rendered with Bioconductor devel.
    • File not found. Learners must open the RStudio project (episode 3) so that the working directory is correct. Check with getwd().
    • Harmless warnings.
      • agglomerateByRank() and agglomerateByRanks() warn that 'rclr' includes negative values when the data already has an rclr table. Episode 5 uses this to teach “agglomerate first, then transform”.
    • Random numbers. PERMANOVA, dbRDA, MaAsLin 3, k-means and the train/test split use random numbers, so learners’ p-values can differ slightly from the lesson. This is expected; the conclusions do not change.
    • Run time. Episode 9 takes about a minute; challenge 2 trains three more random forests.
    • Masked functions. Loading mikropml (through caret) masks mia::cluster(). Load mia last, or call mia::cluster() explicitly, if both are needed in one session.
